en: The Sūtra on the Great Meaning of Birth Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlaguṇabhadra, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial and Acting Minister of the Court of Reception,
Dharma-Master Subject Śīlaguṇabhadra, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Kuru together with a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying alone in a certain place, and in the middle of the night, a reflection arose in his mind:

“The phenomena that arise through conditions are profound in meaning and difficult to comprehend; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessing right and universal knowledge, is well able to proclaim them.”
Having formed this thought, at the break of dawn, he left his original location and went to where the Buddha was.
Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet; having extended his greetings, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

While staying alone in a certain place, a thought arose in my mind at midnight: "The phenomena produced by conditions are profoundly deep and difficult to understand; I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain them for me."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"It is so, it is so. This dharma of dependent origination is profound and subtle, difficult to see, difficult to understand, and difficult to contemplate. Only those who are noble ones, possessing skillful wisdom, can discern it; it is not something that the ignorant can comprehend."

Why is this? Because ignorant sentient beings die in this world and are reborn in another; thus they cycle through saṃsāra, all due to their failure to understand the principle of dependent origination.
Ānanda! You should know that all phenomena arise through the successive production of causes and conditions; therefore, saṃsāra cannot be severed.
As for the phenomenon of dependent origination, it refers to old age and death: with birth as a condition, there is old age and death.
If the dharma of birth did not exist, how could aging and death exist?
Thus, through the condition of birth, things arise in succession.

That is to say: by reason of aquatic beings, aquatic beings are born; by reason of birds, birds are born; by reason of various species, those species are born; and so on, up to human beings being born by reason of humans. By virtue of these conditions, those various sentient beings arise through mutual causes and conditions.

Ānanda! You should know that this phenomenon of birth is a false and deceptive dharma, not ultimate. Because of this accumulation, this cause, this production, and these conditions, there is old age and death; therefore, old age and death are likewise not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what is the condition for the phenomenon of birth?
It is the phenomenon of existence that serves as its condition.
Because existence exists, the phenomenon of birth arises."
If there were no phenomena, how could the phenomena of arising exist?
Therefore, as previously explained, phenomena exist such that the various classes of beings are produced from one another in succession, without interruption.

Ānanda! You should know that these phenomena which exist are illusory and not ultimate; since they arise through this accumulation, this cause, this origination, and this condition, these phenomena that arise are likewise not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what is the condition for the phenomenon of existence (*bhava*)?
It is the phenomenon of grasping (*upādāna*) that serves as its condition.
By means of the phenomenon of grasping, the phenomenon of existence arises."
If the grasping of dharmas were non-existent, how could any dharma be obtained? Ānanda!

You should know that this grasping of dharmas is a false and illusory dharma, not ultimate. This accumulation, this cause, this arising, and this condition give rise to the existence of dharmas; because of this, those existing dharmas are likewise not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what serves as the condition for grasping (*upādāna*)?
It is the phenomenon of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that serves as its condition.
Because craving exists, grasping arises."
If there were no craving for phenomena, how could there be grasping? Ānanda, you should know that because of this craving as a condition, seeking arises;

with seeking as a condition, acquisition occurs; because of acquisition, the mind lacks certainty; due to this lack of certainty, there is no contentment; because the inner mind lacks contentment, joyous greed arises; with greed as a condition, the view of self arises; once the view of self has arisen, there is attachment to what is grasped; with attachment as a condition, the mind becomes distracted; due to distraction, false speech, litigation, and strife arise, along with the wielding of weapons and mutual punishment; through these causes and conditions, one then performs various unwholesome karmas.
All such karmas arise by means of distraction;
if there were no distraction, these karmas would not arise.
What serves as the condition for this phenomenon of distraction?
What is called "clinging" serves as the condition.
Because of clinging, the mind becomes distracted;
if there were no clinging, how could distraction arise?
What serves as the condition for this clinging to phenomena?
It is the view of a self that serves as the condition for the arising of clinging;
if the view of a self were absent, there would be no clinging.
With what as its condition does this view of self arise regarding phenomena?
It is said that with joy and craving as conditions, the view of self arises;
if joy and craving are absent, then the view of self is absent.
What serves as the condition for this dharma of joy and craving?
It is internal lack of contentment that serves as the condition.
Because of this lack of contentment, there arises joy and craving.
If the internal mind experiences satiety, joy and craving will not arise.
With what as a condition does this internal lack of satiety occur?
It is conditioned by lack of certainty.
Because it is not fixed, there is no sense of satiety;
if the mind were fixed, satiety would arise.
What is the condition for this state of non-fixity?
That which is called "having something to be attained" serves as a condition.
Because there is attainment, the mind is not settled;
if there is nothing to be attained, the mind is settled.
What serves as the condition for this dharma of apprehension?
It is so-called longing that serves as the condition.
Because of longing, there is apprehension.
If there is no longing, then there is nothing to be obtained.
Thus, all phenomena arise through the mutual conditionality of craving and longing.

One should know that the phenomenon of craving is of two kinds, namely craving for sensory desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) and craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*); it is from these two phenomena that all faults arise.

Ānanda! You should know that this dharma of craving is a false dharma and not ultimate; it is accumulated by this, caused by this, produced by this, and arises conditioned by this, giving rise to the dharma of grasping. Because of this, the dharma of grasping is also not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what is the condition for craving for the Dharma?
It is the experience of the Dharma that serves as its condition.
By virtue of the condition of experience, craving for the Dharma arises."
If there were no craving for the phenomena of feeling, how could they exist? Ānanda!

You should know that these phenomena of feeling are illusory and not ultimate; because they arise through accumulation, cause, birth, and conditions, they give rise to craving. Therefore, the phenomenon of craving is likewise not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what is the condition for the phenomenon of sensation?
It is contact that serves as its condition.
By reason of contact as a condition, the phenomenon of sensation arises."
If there were no dharma of contact, how could there be the dharma of feeling?

Thus, with eye-contact as a condition, various feelings arise internally—namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; likewise, with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions, various feelings arise internally.
"All these feelings arise with contact as their condition.

Ānanda, you should know that this contact is a deceptive phenomenon and not ultimate. Because this contact arises, is caused by this, is produced by this, and has this as its condition, feelings come to be; therefore, feelings, too, are not ultimate."
"Furthermore, with what as condition does contact arise?
It is with the six sense bases as condition.
From the condition of the six sense bases, contact arises."
If the six sense bases were non-existent, how could contact exist? Ānanda!

You should know that these phenomena of the six sense bases are false and not ultimate; because they arise from this accumulation, this cause, this birth, and this condition, contact also is not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what is the condition for the six sense bases?
They are conditioned by name-and-form.
Because of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise."
If name-and-form did not exist, how could the six sense bases arise?

This "name-and-form" refers to the accumulation of material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) and mental phenomena (citta-ādi-dharma); this name-and-form and that consciousness (vijñāna-dharma) act as mutual conditions for one another, and through their conjunction, they arise together—this is what constitutes name-and-form.

Ānanda! You should know that the phenomena of name-and-form are illusory and not ultimate; because of this accumulation, this cause, this arising, and this condition, the six sense bases come to be, and therefore the six sense bases are also not ultimate.
"Furthermore, what serves as the condition for this phenomenon of name-and-form (nāmarūpa)?
It is the phenomenon of consciousness (vijñāna) that serves as its condition.
Because of the phenomenon of consciousness, there is name-and-form."
If there were no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), how could consciousness (*vijñāna*) exist?

This consciousness, at the very first moment of taking birth within the mother’s womb, depends upon the *kalala*; once the factors of consciousness are fully present, they neither increase nor decrease. Because consciousness serves as a condition, the various aggregates (*skandha*) arise; thus, name-and-form becomes complete and perfect. One should know that this consciousness and that name-and-form act as mutual conditions for their arising.

"Furthermore, it should be known that this consciousness has name-and-form as its condition; therefore, consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.
Because of this, the fruit of suffering arises; once the fruit of suffering has arisen, there is the continuous succession of old age and death."
Through this accumulation, this cause, and this arising, with this as condition, the fruit of suffering is a deceptive phenomenon and not ultimate.

By such causes and conditions, consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; and in this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You should now know that all speech and the paths of speech, as well as non-speech and the paths of non-speech, and that which is produced and the path by which it is produced—these two kinds of things are both not apart from name-and-form (nāmarūpa)."
Ānanda! If one understands in this way, one abides in the vision of equality; this is called thoroughly comprehending the dharma of dependent origination.
This dharma of dependent origination is the fundamental dharma of all Buddhas, the eye of all Buddhas, and the destination to which all Buddhas return.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these words of praise:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have well expounded this Dharma, which brings benefit and happiness to both myself and all the bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I shall now teach you the Dharma of non-appropriation; you should listen attentively and receive it with care, reflecting upon it with proper mindfulness."
Ānanda! You should know that apart from the mark of self, there is no dharma of reception. Why is this?
If there were a self in my teaching, then the phenomena of grasping would arise accordingly;
but since one has realized that the self is empty, how could there be a grasper? Ānanda!
When both the self and the phenomena of sensation have ceased, there is nothing at all, and one abides in the vision of equality.
"Ānanda! There are three kinds of sensations: pleasant sensation, painful sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation."

Regarding what is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*): it consists of the feeler and the phenomena felt. If one can thoroughly comprehend these two as phenomena subject to disintegration, then there is no pleasant feeling; therefore, there are no phenomena to be felt.
Why is this? You should know that pleasant feeling is an impermanent phenomenon; once pleasant feeling has ceased, the mark of a self is abandoned.
Since the mark of a self no longer exists, who is there to experience it?

"Furthermore, regarding painful feeling—namely, the one who feels and the phenomena that are felt—if one can thoroughly comprehend these two as being subject to disintegration and destruction, then there is no painful feeling; therefore, there are no phenomena to be felt."
Why is this? You should know that painful sensation is an impermanent phenomenon; once painful sensation has ceased, one is immediately free from the mark of a self.
Since the mark of a self no longer exists, who is there to experience it?
"Furthermore, it is the same for sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.

Regarding what is called 'the feeler' and 'the phenomena of feeling,' there are two kinds. If one can thoroughly comprehend that these two are phenomena subject to disintegration, then one attains equanimity toward the three states—pain, pleasure, and that which is neither painful nor pleasant—and thus there is no longer any sensation."

Why is this? These three types of sensation are all impermanent and ultimately devoid of reality; once these sensations have ceased, one is immediately free from the mark of self. Since the mark of self does not exist, how could there be a feeler?
“Ānanda! What do you think? You should know that all sensations arise from the mind;
because the mind does not undergo transformation, there is no internal experiencer of sensation. Because phenomena have no substantial reality, there is no external object of sensation.”
Therefore, Ānanda!
One who understands in this way abides in the view of equality; one who abides in this view has fully realized the dharma of non-appropriation.
This dharma of non-appropriation is the fundamental dharma of all Buddhas, the eye of all Buddhas, and the destination to which all Buddhas resort.
At that time, Ānanda further praised him, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have well expounded this Dharma!”
"Having heard this, we shall believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I shall now explain for you the Dharma of non-self; listen closely and receive it with care, attending well to it, and keep it in mind through reflection."

Ānanda! To fully comprehend that feeling is non-existent is to be free from the view of self; having abandoned the view of self, one abides in the vision of equality. One who abides in this vision is equal regarding all signs. By virtue of this equality, there is no further arising in the world. Having comprehended non-arising, one realizes: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

Ānanda! You should know that when the view of self does not arise and one dwells in the view of equality, one thus attains the excellent liberation of mind; being without knowledge or views and without anything to be attained, one is free from all conceptualization, thoroughly penetrating both attainment and non-attainment, as well as neither having attainment nor lacking attainment.

Having realized this, one has neither knowledge nor vision regarding speech and the path of speech, nor non-speech and the path of non-speech, nor that which is produced and the path by which it is produced.

Having thus realized this, one immediately abandons the view of self and abides in the view of equality; knowing things as they truly are, this is precisely what is called "penetrating the dharma of non-self.
This is the fundamental dharma of all Buddhas, the eye of all Buddhas, and the destination to which all Buddhas resort.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Ānanda spoke again in praise:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have well expounded this Dharma!”
"Having heard this, we shall believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"I shall now proclaim it for you once again. You should listen attentively and receive it with care; attend to it well and keep it in mind through reflection."

Ānanda! You should know that no characteristic of form can be apprehended; one should understand it as it truly is, free from all grasping at a self. Having understood this, one contemplates this body as being perishable, unreal, and not something to be cherished.

Observing in this manner, one becomes free from all signs of form and does not give rise to self-clinging; once the notion of a self has been extinguished, one realizes that this body is perishable and unreal, thereby attaining the vision of equanimity.
One who dwells in this vision thoroughly realizes that all aggregates are empty. Since the aggregates are empty, how could there be any perception of a self or of the characteristics of form?
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"
There are seven bases where consciousness dwells and two bases that are not bases for consciousness.
As for the seven bases of consciousness:
first, there are sentient beings who possess form, with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; this is the first base where consciousness dwells.
If there are sentient beings possessing form who have diverse bodies but a single perception—namely, the gods of the first dhyāna—heaven—this is the second abode of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings possessing form who have a single body but diverse perceptions—namely, the gods of the second dhyāna—heaven—this is the third abode of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings with form who possess a single body and a single perception—namely, those in the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna—this is the fourth abode of consciousness.

If there are no sentient beings with form, where all perceptions of form are transcended and there is only a single expanse of space—namely, the Heaven of Infinite Space—this is the fifth abode of consciousness.

If there is no form and no sentient beings, and if in all those places one is free from the perception of emptiness, such that there is solely consciousness—namely, the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness—this is the sixth dwelling place of consciousness.

If there is no form and no sentient beings, and all those places are devoid of consciousness and infinite, being entirely nothing at all—namely, the Heaven of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana)—this is the seventh abode of consciousness.
Ānanda! There are two kinds of places that are not abodes for consciousness:
namely, where there are beings with form, such as the Heaven of Non-perception; this is the first place that is not an abode for consciousness.

If there were no form and no sentient beings, yet they were all free from the sphere of nothingness and dwelt in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—that is, the gods of the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this constitutes the second station of consciousness.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In this way, there are sentient beings with form who possess various bodies and various perceptions; this is the first station of consciousness."
"You monks! You should understand this as it truly is:
whether walking, sitting, or speaking, you should always praise these Dharma-gates and extensively explain them in detail for others."

In this manner, up to the seventh consciousness as a place of abiding, and likewise for the two non-consciousness-abiding dharma-gates, it is also thus. Whether walking, sitting, or speaking, one should always praise what the Buddhas have taught, give rise to pure faith, and understand it according to reality;
if one understands it thus, one immediately attains the fruit of an Arhat through liberation by wisdom.
"Furthermore, Ānanda,
you should know that there are eight doors of liberation:
namely, when one has internal perception of forms and observes external forms, this is the first liberation.
If one, being internally without the perception of form, perceives external forms, this is the second liberation.
If one realizes for oneself the pure liberation through the body, this is the third liberation.

If, having attained purity and being free from all perceptions of form, one contemplates a single expanse of space as being without limit or boundary, and this contemplation is perfected, this constitutes the fourth liberation: the sphere of infinite space.

If one transcends the sphere of infinite space, one should contemplate consciousness; since consciousness is also infinite, when this contemplation is accomplished, it is called the fifth liberation: the sphere of infinite consciousness.

If, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, one contemplates that everything is utterly non-existent, and this contemplation is perfected, this constitutes the sixth liberation: the sphere of nothingness.

Having emerged from the sphere of nothingness, one should contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; when this contemplation is accomplished, it constitutes the seventh liberation: the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If, having transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells in the samādhi of the cessation of perception and feeling, and having personally realized it with the body, this is the eighth liberation, the cessation of perception and feeling; these are called the eight doors of liberation.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You should now know, O bhikṣus! The seven stations of consciousness, the two non-stations of consciousness, and the dharma-gate of the eight liberations that I have previously taught."
As I have taught, you should understand these things as they truly are, always rejoicing in them with praise, and furthermore, practice accordingly.
If one attains complete mastery of these Dharma gates, one will obtain the fruit of Arhatship, which consists of two kinds of liberation.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and all the bhikṣus were filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Great Meaning of Birth Spoken by the Buddha.
